criterion_notes.c1: Examines domestic drinking water supply and household water consumption across eight rural and peri-urban community water supply systems (WSSs) managed by Water Users' Associations (WUAs) in Restrepo and Cali, Colombia.
criterion_notes.c2: Passes the plain/broad wording of Criterion 2, but FAILS the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain wording ('Examines a legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory or governance factor'), the paper descriptively examines WUA institutional/governance capacity across eight rural and peri-urban WSSs (staffing/plumber counts, volunteer vs. professionalized WUA management, presence of a supplier Water Use Efficiency Programme [WUEP], and self-financing vs. subsidy reliance) alongside socio-economic factors. However, under the active 2026-10-13 narrow clarification, Criterion 2 requires an empirical examination of a rule-type mechanism directly governing service access (eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation/tenure requirements, tariff/cost-recovery rules, discretion/accommodation, enforcement, or utility ownership/regulatory structure governing access). Here, all eight systems are community-managed WUAs, national laws (Law 142 of 1994; Decree 1076 of 2015) appear only as unanalysed macro-governance background, low water prices/billing are mentioned only qualitatively in passing as O&M context rather than analysed as tariff rules governing access, and the empirical explanatory analysis tests socio-economic/demographic factors (household size, education, age, occupation, rural vs. peri-urban distance to Cali) and operational water-conservation/leak-control practices on water use efficiency.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary empirical evidence combining a cross-sectional survey of 965 households, online/in-person workshops and interviews with WUA leaders and staff, and 24-hour volumetric water-balance flow measurements across eight WSSs.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports water quantity outcomes at both system and household levels: system water supplied per capita (W, in litres/person/day), physical water losses between intake and storage tank (%), and self-reported/perceived domestic indoor water consumption (in lpcd).
criterion_notes.c5: Clearly identifies the population and units of analysis (965 households connected to 4 rural WSSs in Restrepo and 4 peri-urban WSSs in Cali, plus the 8 WSSs at system level), exposures (socio-economic contextual factors: household size, education, age, occupation, peri-urban vs. rural location/distance; and descriptive WUA operational/staffing features), outcomes (perceived domestic water use in lpcd, system water supplied per capita in lpcd, and supply-to-use efficiency ratios), and study design (cross-sectional household survey with system-level volumetric flow measurements and qualitative WUA interviews).
criterion_notes.c6: Published in English (questionnaire translated from Spanish to English by the authors).

evidence_quotes.quote: Based on an extensive survey of approximately 1000 households in four rural and four peri-urban communities in the Valle del Cauca Department, Colombia, we identified the factors underlying inefficient water supply and use.
Therefore, to fill this gap, this study aims to identify contextual factors that influence water use by employing a multilevel framework household and water supply levels.
Household size, education level, age and occupation were found to be critical factors influencing end water use and water supply.

An exception is system 1R, which distributes water to a larger area for a larger population across different sectors of the water supply system. The water users’ association in this system comprises several people on the board, although the majority serve voluntarily.

A total of 965 rural and peri-urban households were sampled, and the rate of response was 96%. The sample size represented approximately 20% of domestic water users from the each of WSSs located in the peri-urban zone of Cali and rural Restrepo.
We used the water supplied (measured at the storage tank) and water used at the household level in liters per person per day (lpcd) to determine household level system efficiency.

raw_response.exposure: Household socio-economic and demographic contextual factors (household size, education level, age, occupation) and geographic zone/distance from city (peri-urban Cali vs. rural Restrepo), plus descriptive WUA operational characteristics (staffing/plumbers, flow metering, Water Use Efficiency Programme presence)
raw_response.outcome: Perceived household indoor domestic water consumption (lpcd), system-level water supplied per capita (litres/person/day), physical water losses from intake to storage tank (%), and ratio of perceived water use to water supplied
raw_response.population_and_sample: 965 domestic water-user households (one adult per household) randomly sampled across 8 community-managed water supply systems (4 rural systems in Restrepo, n=191; 4 peri-urban systems in Cali, n=774) in Valle del Cauca Department, Colombia, plus system-level observations across the 8 WSSs
raw_response.rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure) per the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification. Although the study empirically measures domestic water consumption (lpcd) and system water supply per capita across 965 households and 8 community water supply systems in Colombia, its explanatory focus is on socio-economic/behavioral determinants of water demand efficiency (household size, education, age, occupation, rural vs. peri-urban proximity) and technical/operational system losses. National water regulations (Law 142 of 1994; Decree 1076 of 2015) are cited only as unanalysed background, all eight studied systems share the same WUA ownership form, and descriptive discussions of WUA volunteer staffing, flow metering, and supplier Water Use Efficiency Programmes reflect operational/conservation management capacity rather than a rule-type legal, administrative, tariff, or regulatory mechanism directly governing household service access. Under the plain literal wording of Criterion 2, the descriptive comparison of WUA governance/management capacity would support inclusion.
raw_response.study_design: Cross-sectional household survey combined with 24-hour system-level volumetric water-balance measurements and qualitative WUA workshops/interviews (mixed-methods socio-hydrological case study)
